hook: PyTorch's autograd is a graph walk you can write in about 100 lines of Python. Let's write it and match PyTorch to six decimals.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Every gradient PyTorch has ever computed for you came from a graph walk you can write in about 100 lines. Let's write it.

0:15 QUESTION — When you call loss.backward() on GPT-2, something has to visit 124 million parameters in the right order and hand each one its gradient. If you can't build that machinery, you can't debug it when a gradient comes back None or NaN.

1:00 INTUITION — Every number remembers who made it. A Value is a scalar plus a pointer to its parents and a tiny function that knows how to push gradient back to them. Backward is: sort the graph, walk it in reverse, call each tiny function. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Chain rule on a graph: dL/dx = sum over children c of dL/dc * dc/dx. Local rules: for c = a + b, dc/da = 1, so a.grad += c.grad. For c = a * b, a.grad += b.data * c.grad and b.grad += a.data * c.grad. For t = tanh(n), n.grad += (1 - t^2) * t.grad. The += matters, a node used twice gets gradient from both paths. Seed: L.grad = 1.

5:30 CODE — class Value: __init__(self, data, _children=(), _op=''), fields data, grad=0.0, _prev=set(_children), _backward=lambda: None. Write __add__, __mul__, tanh, each defining a closure _backward. Then backward(): build topo order with a DFS over _prev, set self.grad = 1.0, loop reversed(topo) calling v._backward(). Add __radd__, __rmul__, __neg__, __sub__, __pow__ for ints, exp, __truediv__ as a * b**-1.

9:00 RECEIPT — Build the classic neuron: x1=2, x2=0, w1=-3, w2=1, b=6.8813735870195432, o = tanh(x1*w1 + x2*w2 + b). Same expression with torch.tensor(..., dtype=torch.double, requires_grad=True). Assert abs(o.data - 0.7071) < 1e-4 and, for each leaf, abs(mine.grad - torch_leaf.grad.item()) < 1e-6. Expected grads: x1 -1.5, w1 1.0, x2 0.5, w2 0.0.
10:30 MEASURE — Show the bug: a = Value(3); b = a + a; b.backward(). With = instead of +=, a.grad is 1. With +=, it is 2. Print both side by side.
11:30 TAKEAWAY — Autograd is a topological sort plus local derivatives plus +=. Interview line: reverse-mode AD costs one backward pass per scalar output, which is why we train with a scalar loss.
12:00 NEXT — Next: micrograd, part 2: neurons to an MLP.
key_math: dL/dx = sum_c (dL/dc)(dc/dx);  c=a+b: da += dc;  c=a*b: da += b*dc, db += a*dc;  t=tanh(n): dn += (1-t^2) dt
code_task: micrograd/engine.py: class Value(data, _children=(), _op='') with __add__, __mul__, __pow__(int|float), tanh, exp, relu, backward(). All scalars, no tensors. backward() does topo sort via DFS then reversed traversal.
receipt: For the expression o = tanh(x1*w1 + x2*w2 + b), build the same graph in torch with dtype=torch.double and requires_grad=True; for each leaf assert abs(v.grad - t.grad.item()) < 1e-6. Expected: x1.grad=-1.5, w1.grad=1.0, x2.grad=0.5, w2.grad=0.0, o=0.7071.
gotchas: Using = instead of += in _backward, so reused nodes lose gradient; forgetting to wrap Python numbers (2 * v) so __rmul__ fails; calling _backward in forward order instead of reversed topo order
interview_q: Why does reverse-mode autodiff dominate deep learning instead of forward-mode? Answer: we have millions of inputs and one scalar loss; reverse mode gets all input gradients in one backward pass costing a small constant times the forward, while forward mode needs one pass per input.
explainer: Here is one neuron written as a graph. Two inputs, two weights, a bias, a sum, and a tanh at the end.
Every box stores two numbers. The value from the forward pass, and a gradient slot that starts at zero.
Backward starts at the output. We set its gradient to one, because the output changes one for one with itself.
Then we walk the graph in reverse topological order, so every node is finished before its parents need it.
At tanh, the local derivative is one minus the output squared. Half, here. We multiply and pass it down.
A plus node copies gradient to both inputs unchanged. A times node swaps: each side gets the other side's value.
When one value feeds two places, gradients from both paths add up. That is why every update is plus equals.
Final gradients. x1 gets minus one point five, w1 gets one. And PyTorch prints the exact same numbers.
explainer_visuals: A left-to-right DAG: leaf boxes x1, w1, x2, w2, b feeding * and + nodes into a tanh node, each box showing its data value.
Each box splits into a top half 'data' filled in and a bottom half 'grad' shown as 0.0 in gray.
The tanh box's grad slot flashes and fills with 1.0; a red pulse sits on it.
Nodes get numbered right to left by a topo sort; a cursor moves along the numbers.
Formula 1 - t^2 = 0.5 appears over the tanh edge; the red pulse travels to the sum node, which shows grad 0.5.
Pulse splits at + into two equal arrows; at * the arrows cross over, labeled 'b.data * grad' and 'a.data * grad'.
A node a with two outgoing edges; two red pulses come back and stack into one grad bar labeled +=.
Leaf grads appear; a split screen shows a torch printout with matching values and a green check.
short: The += bug demo (MEASURE). Caption: 'One character breaks autograd: = vs +='
yt_title: Autograd from Scratch in Python: micrograd matches PyTorch exactly
x_post: PyTorch autograd is a topo sort, local derivatives, and +=. Built micrograd's Value class and matched torch grads to 1e-6. The bug everyone hits: = instead of += when a node is reused. Code + video: [link]
linkedin: Built a scalar autograd engine from scratch today (micrograd lineage): Value with +, *, tanh and a topological backward. Gradients match PyTorch float64 to 1e-6 on a test neuron. The lesson: a node used twice must accumulate gradient, and one '=' instead of '+=' silently breaks it.

hook: A neural net is just your autograd engine plus a loop. Forty lines turns a scalar Value class into a classifier.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Last time we built autograd for single numbers. Today forty more lines turns it into a neural net that learns two moons.

0:15 QUESTION — nn.Linear, nn.Module, optimizer.step, zero_grad. These are the four ideas behind every training script, including the one that trained Llama 3. We rebuild each one on top of our own engine so none of them is magic.

1:00 INTUITION — A neuron is a weighted vote plus a squash. A layer is many neurons reading the same input. An MLP is layers in a row. Training is: forward, loss, backward, nudge every weight against its gradient, clear the gradients, repeat. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Neuron: out = tanh(sum_i w_i x_i + b). MLP: x -> L1 -> L2 -> L3. Loss for labels y in {-1, +1}: hinge, mean(relu(1 - y_i * score_i)), plus alpha * sum(w^2) for L2 regularization. Update: w <- w - lr * dL/dw. Why zero_grad: our += accumulates across steps, so we reset to 0 before each backward.

5:00 CODE — class Module: zero_grad() sets p.grad = 0 for p in parameters(). class Neuron(Module): __init__(nin) makes w = [Value(random.uniform(-1,1)) for _ in range(nin)], b = Value(0); __call__(x) returns sum((wi*xi for wi,xi in zip(w,x)), b).relu() or tanh. class Layer(nin, nout), class MLP(nin, [16,16,1]). Data: sklearn.datasets.make_moons(n_samples=100, noise=0.1), y mapped to -1/+1. Train loop 100 steps, lr = 1.0 - 0.9*k/100.

9:00 RECEIPT — Port the same MLP to torch with identical initial weights (copy each Value.data into nn.Linear weight and bias, float64). One forward and backward on the full batch. Assert every parameter gradient matches to 1e-6: torch.testing.assert_close(torch.tensor([p.grad for p in mlp.parameters()]), torch.cat([p.grad.flatten() for p in tmodel.parameters()]), atol=1e-6, rtol=0) with parameters flattened in the same order. Then training accuracy hits 100% on moons.
10:30 MEASURE — Plot the decision boundary every 20 steps; loss curve; parameter count 337 for MLP(2, [16, 16, 1]).

11:30 TAKEAWAY — nn.Module is a parameter registry, the optimizer is a for loop, and zero_grad exists because gradients accumulate. Interview line: forgetting zero_grad gives you gradient accumulation across steps, which is a feature for big batches and a bug otherwise.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Bigram language model by counting.
key_math: neuron: y = phi(w . x + b);  hinge loss L = mean_i relu(1 - y_i s_i) + alpha ||w||^2;  SGD: w <- w - eta dL/dw
code_task: micrograd/nn.py: Module.parameters()/zero_grad(); Neuron(nin, nonlin=True); Layer(nin, nout); MLP(nin, nouts). MLP(2,[16,16,1]) has 337 Values. Train on make_moons(100) with hinge loss and L2, full batch, 100 SGD steps.
receipt: Copy initial weights into an equivalent float64 torch nn.Sequential(Linear(2,16), ReLU, Linear(16,16), ReLU, Linear(16,1)); after one forward/backward on the same batch, torch.testing.assert_close on the flattened gradient vectors with atol=1e-6, rtol=0. Then assert training accuracy == 1.0 after 100 steps.
gotchas: Forgetting zero_grad so gradients pile up and loss explodes; last layer with a nonlinearity, so scores are clipped and hinge loss cannot separate; parameter ordering differs between your MLP and torch when comparing gradients (torch Linear weight is (out, in))
interview_q: What does optimizer.zero_grad() do and what happens if you skip it? Answer: PyTorch accumulates .grad with +=, so without zeroing each step uses the sum of all past gradients; it is intentional, because it lets you do gradient accumulation over micro-batches.
explainer: A neuron takes a list of inputs, multiplies each by its own weight, adds a bias, then squashes the result.
A layer is a row of neurons all reading the same inputs. Each neuron has its own weights.
Stack layers and you have an MLP. Ours is two inputs, sixteen, sixteen, then one score out.
The data is two interleaved moons of points. Red points mean minus one, blue points mean plus one.
Each step we push every point through, measure a hinge loss, and call backward on our own engine.
Then each weight moves a little against its gradient. Before the next step we reset every gradient to zero.
Watch the decision boundary. At first it is a straight smear. By step one hundred it wraps both moons.
Same weights in PyTorch give the same gradients, number for number. Our forty lines are the real thing.
explainer_visuals: Three input dots with arrows labeled w1, w2, w3 into a circle with sigma and a small ReLU curve inside.
The neuron duplicates into a vertical column of 16 circles, every input wired to every circle.
Three columns 2, 16, 16, 1 with dense wiring; a counter in the corner reads 337 parameters.
Scatter plot of make_moons, 100 points, two crescents in red and blue.
Points flow left to right through the MLP; a loss number appears; red gradient arrows flow back through the wires.
Weight values tick up or down; a broom icon wipes all grad slots back to 0.0.
A shaded background contour morphs over training steps from a flat split into a curved boundary hugging both crescents.
Two gradient columns side by side, ours and torch, with matching digits and a green check.
short: Decision boundary morph (MEASURE). Caption: 'A neural net trained on 100 lines of my own autograd'
yt_title: Build a Neural Network from Scratch on Your Own Autograd Engine
x_post: nn.Module is a parameter list, optimizer.step is a for loop, zero_grad exists because grads accumulate. Built an MLP on my own scalar autograd, grads match torch to 1e-6, 100% on two moons. Code + video: [link]
linkedin: Extended my from-scratch autograd into Neuron, Layer and MLP classes and trained a 337-parameter net to 100% accuracy on two moons. Gradients match an equivalent PyTorch model to 1e-6. Writing zero_grad yourself is the fastest way to understand why it exists.

hook: The first language model is a 27 by 27 table of counts. It scores 2.45 nats per character. Everything after must beat it.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — The simplest language model is a 27 by 27 table of counts. It gets 2.45 nats per character. Remember that number.

0:15 QUESTION — GPT-4 and a bigram table do the same job: output a probability distribution over the next token. The bigram is the baseline every model in this series has to beat, and its loss, average negative log likelihood, is the exact loss we will train GPT with.

1:00 INTUITION — Read 32,033 names. Every time you see letter a followed by letter b, add one to cell (a, b). Normalize each row and you have P(next | current). To generate, start at the boundary token, roll a weighted die from that row, repeat until you roll the boundary again. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — P(c_{t+1} | c_t) = N[c_t, c_{t+1}] / sum_j N[c_t, j]. Likelihood of the data is the product of these. Log likelihood is the sum of logs, because products of small numbers underflow. Loss = NLL = -(1/n) sum log P. Lower is better, 0 is perfect, log(27) = 3.296 is uniform guessing. Add-one smoothing: N + 1 so no probability is exactly 0 and no loss is infinite.

5:30 CODE — words = open('names.txt').read().splitlines(). chars = sorted(set(''.join(words))); stoi with '.' at index 0. N = torch.zeros((27, 27), dtype=torch.int32). For each word, for ch1, ch2 in zip(['.'] + list(w), list(w) + ['.']): N[stoi[ch1], stoi[ch2]] += 1. P = (N + 1).float(); P /= P.sum(1, keepdim=True). Sample with torch.multinomial(P[ix], 1, generator=g). Compute NLL over all 228,146 bigrams.

9:00 RECEIPT — assert torch.allclose(P.sum(1), torch.ones(27)). NLL over the full dataset with +1 smoothing prints about 2.454. Cross-check: F.cross_entropy(torch.log(P)[xs], ys) gives the same number to 1e-6, because log P rows are already log-softmaxed.
10:30 MEASURE — Show N as a heatmap with letters on the axes, 20 sampled names (they are bad, that is the point), and the NLL: 2.454 vs uniform 3.296.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — A language model is a conditional distribution and its loss is average negative log likelihood. Interview line: the keepdim=True in the normalize is not cosmetic, without it broadcasting divides columns instead of rows.
12:00 NEXT — Next: The bigram model as a neural net.
key_math: P(b|a) = N[a,b] / sum_j N[a,j];  NLL = -(1/n) sum_i log P(c_{i+1}|c_i);  uniform baseline = ln 27 = 3.296
code_task: bigram_count.py: build N (27, 27) int32 from names.txt with '.' as start/end token; P = (N+1)/rowsum, shape (27, 27); sample(P, g, n=20) via torch.multinomial; nll(P, words) -> float.
receipt: assert torch.allclose(P.sum(dim=1), torch.ones(27)); nll printed approximately 2.454 on all 228,146 bigrams; torch.testing.assert_close(my_nll, F.cross_entropy(P.log()[xs], ys)) to 1e-6.
gotchas: P / P.sum(1) without keepdim=True broadcasts the (27,) sum across rows and normalizes columns, giving plausible-looking garbage; no smoothing means log(0) = -inf and loss = inf on unseen pairs; using separate start and end tokens is fine but changes the table to 28x28, so your numbers will not match
interview_q: What is the cross-entropy loss of a model that predicts uniformly over a vocabulary of size V? Answer: ln V. For 27 characters that is 3.296 nats; for GPT-2's 50,257 tokens it is about 10.82, which is the loss you should see at step 0 with a good init.
explainer: A language model answers one question. Given what came before, how likely is each possible next token?
The simplest past is one character. So we count, for every letter, which letter comes next in thirty two thousand names.
This grid is the whole model. Bright cells are common pairs. N then a is bright. Q then anything but u is dark.
Divide each row by its sum, and each row becomes a probability distribution over the next letter.
To generate, we start at the dot token, roll a weighted die from that row, and follow the result.
To score the model, we take the log probability it gave to each real next letter, and average.
The bigram table scores two point four five. Uniform guessing scores three point three. Lower means less surprised.
explainer_visuals: The phrase 'given the past, P(next)' with a bar chart over 27 letters fading in.
Names scroll by; each adjacent pair lights up and increments a cell in a 27 by 27 grid.
Heatmap of N with letters on both axes; the n-to-a cell and the q row are highlighted.
One row lifts out, its numbers turn into a bar chart that sums to 1.
A die rolls on the dot row, lands on 'k', the cursor jumps to the k row, rolls again.
Under the word 'emma', each transition shows its probability and its log, then an average symbol collects them.
A number line from 0 to 3.3 with markers at 2.45 'bigram' and 3.30 'uniform'.
short: The keepdim bug (CODE). Caption: 'keepdim=True: one argument that silently breaks your model'
yt_title: Bigram Language Model from Scratch: the 2.45 baseline to beat
x_post: The first language model is a 27x27 count table. NLL 2.454 on names vs 3.296 for uniform. Every LLM loss you'll see is this same quantity, average negative log likelihood. Code + video: [link]
linkedin: Built a character bigram language model by counting pairs in 32k names. It reaches 2.454 nats/char NLL versus 3.296 for uniform guessing, and the number matches F.cross_entropy exactly. That NLL is the same loss used to train GPT, so this is the baseline everything else must beat.

hook: Train a one-layer neural net with gradient descent and it rediscovers the count table. Same loss, 2.45, no counting.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — A neural net with one weight matrix, trained by gradient descent, rediscovers our count table. Same 2.45. Never saw a count.

0:15 QUESTION — Counting does not scale. You cannot count every 1000-token context. Neural nets can generalize, but first we have to show they can at least recover the counting answer. This is the frame GPT lives in: inputs, logits, softmax, cross-entropy.

1:00 INTUITION — One-hot encode the current letter, a vector of 26 zeros and a single one. Multiply by W, a 27 by 27 matrix. That just selects one row of W. Treat that row as log-counts, exponentiate, normalize. Gradient descent tunes W until exp(W) is proportional to the counts. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — x = onehot(c_t), shape (27,). logits = x W, shape (27,). probs = softmax(logits) = exp(logits) / sum exp(logits). Loss = -mean log probs[y]. Gradient: dL/dlogits = probs - onehot(y), divided by batch size. So dL/dW = X^T (P - Y) / n. At the optimum the model's average probs match the empirical next-letter frequencies, which is exactly the normalized count row. Regularizer lambda * mean(W^2) plays the role of add-one smoothing, pulling W toward uniform.

6:00 CODE — xs, ys = tensors of 228,146 bigram indices. W = torch.randn((27, 27), generator=g, requires_grad=True). Loop 200 steps: xenc = F.one_hot(xs, num_classes=27).float() shape (228146, 27); logits = xenc @ W; loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, ys) + 0.01 * (W**2).mean(); W.grad = None; loss.backward(); W.data += -50 * W.grad. Learning rate 50 works because the problem is convex and full-batch.

9:00 RECEIPT — Loss converges to about 2.46 to 2.48 with the regularizer, against 2.454 for the counts. Stronger check: P_nn = F.softmax(W, dim=1) and P_count. Print (P_nn - P_count).abs().max(), it falls under 0.01 as you lower the regularizer and train longer. Also assert my manual gradient (F.softmax(logits,1) - F.one_hot(ys,27))/n, then xenc.T @ that, allclose to W.grad at atol 1e-6.
10:30 MEASURE — Loss curve vs step with a dashed line at 2.454; side-by-side heatmaps of exp(W) normalized vs N normalized.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — The neural bigram and the count table are the same model; the neural version just scales to contexts you could never count. Interview line: softmax plus cross-entropy has gradient probs minus one-hot, which is why it is the default output layer.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Embeddings: lookup tables that learn.
key_math: logits = onehot(x) W;  p = softmax(logits);  L = -(1/n) sum log p[y];  dL/dlogits = (p - onehot(y))/n;  dL/dW = X^T (P - Y)/n
code_task: neural_bigram.py: xs, ys int64 (228146,); W (27, 27) float32 requires_grad; forward: F.one_hot(xs, 27).float() @ W -> logits (228146, 27); loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, ys) + lam*(W**2).mean(); full-batch SGD lr=50 for 200+ steps.
receipt: Final loss within 0.03 of the count model's 2.454; (F.softmax(W,1) - P_count).abs().max() < 0.01 with lam=0 and enough steps; torch.testing.assert_close(xenc.T @ ((F.softmax(logits,1) - F.one_hot(ys,27))/n), W.grad) for the unregularized loss.
gotchas: F.one_hot returns int64, so xenc @ W errors until you call .float(); using W.grad.zero_() before the first backward fails because grad is None, set W.grad = None instead; a learning rate of 0.1 looks broken here because full-batch convex problems want very large steps
interview_q: Why is the gradient of softmax cross-entropy with respect to the logits equal to p - y? Answer: d/dz_k of -z_y + log sum exp(z) is -1[k=y] + softmax(z)_k; the log and exp cancel, which makes this combination numerically stable and cheap.
explainer: Same task as last time, predict the next letter. But this time we are not allowed to count.
We write the current letter as a one-hot vector. Twenty six zeros and a single one.
Multiplying a one-hot vector by W does nothing clever. It just picks out one row of W.
We call that row logits. Exponentiate and normalize, and we get a probability for every next letter.
The loss asks how much probability we gave the true next letter. The gradient is predicted minus true.
Two hundred steps of gradient descent later, the loss settles almost exactly at the counting model's two point four five.
Put the two tables side by side. The net learned the counts without ever counting anything.
explainer_visuals: The bigram heatmap from before fades out, replaced by an empty 27 by 27 matrix labeled W.
A column of 27 cells, one lit yellow at the position for 'e'.
The yellow cell draws a line to a single row of W, which slides out of the matrix.
The row becomes bars, then exp makes them positive, then they rescale to sum to 1.
A bar chart with the correct letter highlighted; arrows show p minus onehot, pushing the true bar up and others down.
A loss curve dropping from 3.7 and flattening onto a dashed line labeled 2.454 count model.
Two heatmaps, softmax of W and normalized N, nearly identical, with a small difference map underneath.
short: Side-by-side heatmaps (MEASURE). Caption: 'Gradient descent rediscovered counting'
yt_title: Neural Network Bigram Model: gradient descent rediscovers counting
x_post: One-hot times W just selects a row. Train that row with softmax + cross-entropy and gradient descent recovers the bigram count table: loss 2.46 vs 2.454. The neural frame is what scales to long contexts. Code + video: [link]
linkedin: Trained a single 27x27 weight matrix with softmax cross-entropy and it converged to the bigram count model (2.46 vs 2.454 NLL). I verified my hand-derived gradient, X^T(P - Y)/n, against autograd. Small, but it is the exact output layer every LLM uses.

hook: An embedding layer is a one-hot vector times a matrix, and it learns that vowels belong together without being told.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — An embedding is a one-hot times a matrix. Train it on names and vowels cluster together. Nobody told it what a vowel is.

0:15 QUESTION — Every LLM starts with an embedding table. GPT-2's is 50,257 by 768 and holds 31 percent of its weights. Bengio's 2003 paper is where that idea comes from: give each symbol a learned vector, and let similar symbols share statistical strength.

1:00 INTUITION — Instead of one row per letter of a count table, give each letter a small vector, a point in space. Concatenate the vectors of the last 3 letters, feed them to an MLP, predict the next letter. Letters that behave alike get pushed to nearby points, because that lowers the loss. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — C in R^{27 x d}. Lookup: emb = C[X], shape (B, 3, d), identical to onehot(X) @ C. Flatten to (B, 3d). h = tanh(emb W1 + b1), W1 is (3d, H). logits = h W2 + b2, W2 is (H, 27). Loss = cross-entropy. Parameter count with d=10, H=200: 270 + 6,200 + 5,427 = 11,897. Gradient into C: rows of C only receive gradient where they were looked up, a sparse scatter-add.

5:30 CODE — build_dataset(words, block_size=3) -> X (N, 3) int64, Y (N,). C = torch.randn((27, 10)). emb = C[Xb] shape (32, 3, 10). h = torch.tanh(emb.view(-1, 30) @ W1 + b1) shape (32, 200). logits = h @ W2 + b2 shape (32, 27). loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, Yb). Minibatch of 32, 200k steps, lr 0.1 then 0.01 after 100k. Then a second run with d=2 for plotting.

9:00 RECEIPT — Equivalence: torch.testing.assert_close(F.one_hot(Xb, 27).float() @ C, C[Xb]). Swap your C with nn.Embedding(27, 10) whose weight you copy from C: assert_close(emb_layer(Xb), C[Xb]). Loss: val NLL around 2.17 for d=10, H=200, beating the bigram's 2.45.
10:30 MEASURE — Scatter the 27 learned 2D vectors from the d=2 run, labeled. Point at the vowel cluster a, e, i, o, u and the outlier '.' token. Table: bigram 2.45 vs MLP 2.17.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — An embedding is a learnable lookup, mathematically a one-hot matmul, implemented as an index. Interview line: nn.Embedding backward is a scatter-add into only the rows used, which is why huge vocabularies are cheap to train.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Train, validation, test and overfitting.
key_math: emb = C[X] = onehot(X) C;  h = tanh(flatten(emb) W1 + b1);  logits = h W2 + b2;  params = 27d + (3d+1)H + (H+1)27
code_task: mlp_lm.py: build_dataset(words, block_size=3) -> X (N,3), Y (N,); params C (27,d), W1 (3d,H), b1 (H,), W2 (H,27), b2 (27,); forward(Xb) -> logits (B,27). d=10, H=200 gives 11,897 params.
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(F.one_hot(Xb, 27).float() @ C, C[Xb]); nn.Embedding with weight copied from C gives identical outputs; final val loss approximately 2.17 (below bigram 2.454).
gotchas: emb.view(-1, 30) on a non-contiguous tensor errors, use .reshape or make sure emb came straight from indexing; computing loss with manual exp/log overflows when logits get large, use F.cross_entropy; evaluating loss on one minibatch and reporting it as the model's loss, it is noisy by +/- 0.1
interview_q: Why is an embedding layer implemented as an index instead of a matmul with one-hot vectors? Answer: they are mathematically identical, but indexing is O(B*d) instead of O(B*V*d) and the backward is a sparse scatter-add into only the used rows.
explainer: Last time each letter owned a whole row of probabilities. Now each letter gets a short vector instead, a point in space.
Looking up a vector is the same as multiplying a one-hot by the table. We just skip the zeros.
We grab the vectors for the last three letters and glue them end to end into one input.
A hidden layer with tanh mixes them. An output layer gives logits over twenty seven possible next letters.
Gradients flow all the way back into the table. Only the three rows we used get updated.
After training, the points have moved. The vowels have drifted into one corner, all on their own.
And the loss drops from two point four five for the bigram to about two point one seven.
explainer_visuals: 27 letters fly from a list into a 2D plane, each landing at a random point.
A one-hot vector times matrix C, with the selected row glowing; then the matmul fades and an index arrow replaces it.
Three small vectors for 'e', 'm', 'm' slide together into one long vector of length 30.
The long vector feeds a column of 200 neurons, then a column of 27 output bars.
Red arrows flow backward into C; exactly three rows flash, the others stay gray.
The 2D scatter animates from random to trained; a, e, i, o, u gather in a cluster circled in yellow.
Two bars, bigram 2.45 and MLP 2.17, with an arrow showing the improvement.

yt_title: Embeddings from Scratch: Bengio's MLP language model in PyTorch
x_post: An embedding layer is onehot(x) @ C implemented as C[x]. Built Bengio's 2003 MLP LM: 11.9k params, val loss 2.17 vs 2.45 for bigrams, and the 2D embeddings cluster the vowels unprompted. Code + video: [link]

Plotting a 2D version shows the vowels clustering on their own, which is the whole point of learned embeddings.

hook: Your training loss can go to zero while your model gets worse. The only way to know is a split you never train on.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — I'm going to drive training loss to nearly zero on purpose. The model gets worse. Here's how you catch it.

0:15 QUESTION — Every LLM paper reports validation loss, not training loss, and every lab holds out eval sets the model never sees. Before we scale anything, we need the discipline: three splits, a learning-rate sweep, and the ability to tell underfitting from overfitting from a single plot.

1:00 INTUITION — Training data is the homework, validation is the practice exam you use to tune knobs, test is the real exam you open once. Memorizing homework answers is overfitting: perfect homework, failed exam. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Split words 80/10/10 after a seeded shuffle. Generalization gap = val loss - train loss. LR sweep: lr = 10^e for e in linspace(-3, 0, 1000), one step per lr, record loss. Pick the lr just before the loss curve turns up, about 0.1 here. Capacity: params P vs examples N; when P is large relative to N and training is long, the gap grows.

5:00 CODE — random.seed(42); random.shuffle(words); n1, n2 = int(0.8*len), int(0.9*len). Xtr, Xdev, Xte = build_dataset(...). lre = torch.linspace(-3, 0, 1000); lrs = 10**lre. Loop i over 1000 steps using lrs[i], log loss. Plot loss vs lre. Then overfit experiment: take 32 examples, train the 11.9k-param MLP for 2000 steps, print train loss approaching 0 and val loss rising. Then the honest run: full train set, early stopping on dev loss with patience.

9:00 RECEIPT — Sanity check from Karpathy's recipe: overfit a single batch of 32 to loss under 0.05; if you cannot, there is a bug. Second check: with the full model, dev loss at the best checkpoint should be about 2.17 and test loss evaluated once within 0.02 of dev.
10:30 MEASURE — Two plots. LR finder: loss vs log10(lr), minimum near -1. Overfit: train and val curves diverging, with the early-stopping point marked.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Train loss tells you if you can fit; val loss tells you if you learned; test loss is opened once. Interview line: if you can't overfit one batch, debug the code before touching the hyperparameters.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Activations and dead neurons.
key_math: gap = L_val - L_train;  lr_i = 10^{e_i}, e_i in [-3, 0];  pick lr just left of the loss minimum
code_task: splits.py: split_words(words, seed=42) -> (train, dev, test) at 80/10/10; lr_finder(model, Xtr, Ytr, lrs) -> losses; overfit_batch(model, Xb (32,3), Yb (32,), steps=2000); train_with_early_stopping(model, patience=5) evaluating dev every 1k steps.
receipt: Overfit-one-batch assert: final loss on 32 examples < 0.05. Full run: best dev loss approximately 2.17; test loss computed once and within 0.02 of dev.
gotchas: Splitting the encoded examples instead of the words, so the same name leaks into train and val through overlapping windows; tuning hyperparameters on the test set; reading the LR finder minimum directly instead of backing off by roughly 3 to 10x
interview_q: Your training loss keeps going down but validation loss started rising 2k steps ago. What is happening and what do you do? Answer: overfitting; stop at the best validation checkpoint, then add data, reduce capacity, or add regularization like weight decay or dropout.
explainer: We split the names three ways before training. Eighty percent to learn from, ten to tune on, ten locked away.
First question, what learning rate? We try a thousand of them, from one thousandth up to one, in a single run.
Loss falls, flattens, then explodes. We pick a rate a little before the bottom of that valley.
Now the dangerous experiment. Just thirty two names, twelve thousand parameters, and two thousand training steps on them.
Training loss heads toward zero. The model has memorized those thirty two names, character by character.
But validation loss turns around and climbs. The gap between the two curves is the overfitting.
Early stopping keeps the checkpoint where validation was lowest. That is the model we ship.
explainer_visuals: A bar of 32,033 names splits into three colored segments labeled train, dev, test; a lock icon sits on test.
An x axis from 10^-3 to 10^0 with a moving dot sweeping right, leaving a loss trail.
The loss trail draws a U shape; a marker drops at about 0.1 with a small arrow backing off to the left.
A tiny pile of 32 name cards next to a large network diagram with a 11,897 counter.
A blue train-loss curve plunging toward the x axis.
A red val-loss curve bending upward; the space between red and blue shades in.
A star marks the bottom of the red curve; a save icon pops up at that step.
short: The overfitting curves diverging (MEASURE). Caption: 'Training loss lies'
yt_title: Overfitting, Validation Splits and the LR Finder, from scratch
x_post: Drove training loss to ~0 on 32 names with a 12k-param net. Val loss went up. Then did it properly: 80/10/10 split, LR finder (best ~0.1), early stopping, dev 2.17. Overfit one batch first or you have a bug. Code + video: [link]
linkedin: Built the evaluation discipline for my from-scratch language models: seeded 80/10/10 splits, a 1000-point learning-rate sweep, and early stopping on dev loss. I also overfit 32 examples on purpose to watch the train/val gap open up. The overfit-one-batch test is now the first thing I run on any new model.

hook: Half your tanh neurons can be dead at step zero, and the loss curve won't tell you. A histogram will.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — My network's initial loss is 27. It should be 3.3. And most of my tanh neurons are frozen. Both fixes are one line.

0:15 QUESTION — GPT-2 initializes weights with std 0.02 and scales residual projections by 1/sqrt(2 * n_layer). Those numbers are not folklore. They come from keeping activations in the range where nonlinearities actually have gradient, which is what this episode measures.

1:00 INTUITION — tanh is flat beyond about plus or minus 2. If pre-activations land out there, the gradient 1 - tanh^2 is nearly 0 and the neuron stops learning. ReLU has the same failure on one side: a neuron whose input is always negative is dead forever. GELU is a smooth ReLU that keeps a little gradient for negatives. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Expected initial loss with 27 classes: -ln(1/27) = 3.296. Huge logits make it far bigger, so scale W2 by 0.01 and set b2 = 0. Pre-activation variance: Var(sum_i w_i x_i) = fan_in * Var(w) * Var(x). Keep it 1 with std(w) = gain / sqrt(fan_in). Kaiming gain for tanh is 5/3, for ReLU sqrt(2), because ReLU zeroes half the variance. GELU(x) = x * Phi(x), with Phi the standard normal CDF.

5:30 CODE — Bigger MLP: context 3, d=10, H=200. Before the fix: W1 = torch.randn(30, 200). Record hpreact = embcat @ W1 + b1, h = torch.tanh(hpreact). Plot torch.histc or plt.hist of h.view(-1) and of hpreact. Saturation map: plt.imshow(h.abs() > 0.99, cmap='gray') shape (32, 200). Dead check: columns where (h.abs() > 0.99).all(0). After: W1 *= (5/3) / 30**0.5, W2 *= 0.01, b2 *= 0. Repeat histograms. Then swap tanh for F.relu and F.gelu and count dead units: (h == 0).all(0).sum().

9:00 RECEIPT — Initial loss before fix about 27, after fix 3.29 to 3.30, matching -math.log(1/27) = 3.2958. Gain check: assert torch.nn.init.calculate_gain('tanh') == 5/3. Std check: after the fix, hpreact.std() is about 5/3 times 1 and h saturation fraction (h.abs() > 0.99).float().mean() drops from roughly 0.5+ to under 0.05.
10:30 MEASURE — Before/after histograms of h, the white-pixel saturation map, dead-unit count for tanh vs ReLU vs GELU, and val loss improving from about 2.17 to about 2.10 just from init.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Look at activation histograms, not just the loss curve; most training failures are visible at step zero. Interview line: your initial loss should be ln(V); if it is not, your init is wrong before training even starts.
12:00 NEXT — Next: BatchNorm vs LayerNorm from scratch.
key_math: L_0 = ln V = ln 27 = 3.296;  Var(y) = n_in Var(w) Var(x) -> std(w) = gain/sqrt(n_in);  gain_tanh = 5/3, gain_relu = sqrt(2);  GELU(x) = x Phi(x)
code_task: activations.py: MLP(d=10, H=200, block=3) with init_mode in {'naive','kaiming'}; act in {'tanh','relu','gelu'}; diagnostics(h) -> saturation fraction, dead-unit count over a batch, histograms of hpreact (B,200) and h (B,200).
receipt: Initial loss after fix within 0.01 of -math.log(1/27) = 3.2958 (naive init gives about 27); torch.nn.init.calculate_gain('tanh') == 5/3; saturation fraction (h.abs()>0.99).float().mean() < 0.05 after fix.
gotchas: Calling it a dead neuron when it is only dead on this batch, check across many batches; applying Kaiming gain for ReLU to a tanh net; forgetting the output layer, a correct hidden init with large W2 still gives a huge initial loss
interview_q: What should the initial loss of a freshly initialized LLM with a 50,257-token vocab be, and why do we check it? Answer: about ln(50257) = 10.82; anything much higher means the logits are confidently wrong at init and the first steps are wasted undoing that.
explainer: Before training even starts, the network makes a prediction. With twenty seven letters, the fair loss is three point three.
Ours starts at twenty seven, because the output weights are too big and the logits are confidently wrong.
Now the hidden layer. Here is the tanh curve. Beyond about two, it goes flat.
This histogram shows where our hidden activations land. Most of them are piled up at minus one and plus one.
Each white pixel is a neuron saturated for one example. A full white column is a neuron that never learns.
The fix is to scale the weights by gain over square root of fan in. Five thirds for tanh.
Same histogram after the fix. A smooth hump, almost no saturation, and gradients can flow again.
ReLU dies on the negative side, GELU leaks a little gradient there. Count the dead units for each.
explainer_visuals: A number line with a marker at 3.30 labeled 'ln 27, fair guess'; a second marker far right at 27 labeled 'ours'.
Logit bars that are tall and spiky, one huge bar on the wrong letter.
The tanh curve drawn, with the flat tails shaded red and labeled 'gradient near zero'.
A histogram of h with two tall spikes at -1 and +1 and almost nothing in between.
A 32 by 200 black and white image; one fully white column highlighted.
The formula std = (5/3)/sqrt(30) appears; the weight matrix shrinks visually.
The spiky histogram morphs into a bell-shaped one centered at 0; the saturation image goes mostly black.
Three activation curves side by side, with a bar chart of dead-unit counts beneath them.
short: Spiky histogram morphing into a bell (MEASURE). Caption: 'Your neurons are dead at step zero'
yt_title: Dead Neurons and tanh Saturation: fixing init with Kaiming
x_post: Initial loss should be ln(V). Mine was 27 instead of 3.3, and half my tanh units were saturated. Fix: scale W2 by 0.01 and W1 by (5/3)/sqrt(fan_in). Saturation went from >50% to <5%. Code + video: [link]
linkedin: Measured activation statistics in my from-scratch MLP: naive init gave an initial loss of 27 (should be 3.3) and over half the tanh units saturated. Kaiming-style scaling with the 5/3 tanh gain fixed both and improved val loss. Lesson: check ln(V) and activation histograms before you ever look at a loss curve.

hook: BatchNorm and LayerNorm are the same five lines. Only the averaging axis differs, and that is why transformers use LayerNorm.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — BatchNorm and LayerNorm are the same five lines of code. One argument differs. That argument is why every transformer uses LayerNorm.

0:15 QUESTION — BatchNorm made deep CNNs trainable in 2015. Then the transformer paper used LayerNorm and every LLM since has used LayerNorm or RMSNorm. If you know exactly why, you know what goes wrong with batch statistics at inference time and with variable-length sequences.

1:00 INTUITION — Picture activations as a grid: rows are examples, columns are features. BatchNorm normalizes each column using the batch. LayerNorm normalizes each row using its own features. BatchNorm makes your output depend on who else is in the batch. LayerNorm never does. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Both: y = gamma * (x - mu) / sqrt(var + eps) + beta. BatchNorm on x of shape (N, C): mu, var over dim 0, per feature, biased var (divide by N). Training also updates running_mean = (1 - m) running_mean + m mu with m = 0.1, and running_var with the unbiased batch var. At eval, use running stats. LayerNorm on (..., C): mu, var over the last dim, per example, biased var, same in train and eval. eps = 1e-5 for both PyTorch defaults.

5:30 CODE — def batchnorm_forward(x, gamma, beta, running_mean, running_var, training, momentum=0.1, eps=1e-5): x (N, C); if training: mu = x.mean(0); var = x.var(0, unbiased=False); update running stats with x.var(0, unbiased=True); else use running stats. def layernorm_forward(x, gamma, beta, eps=1e-5): mu = x.mean(-1, keepdim=True); var = x.var(-1, keepdim=True, unbiased=False). Insert BatchNorm after the first linear in the MLP LM and drop b1, since BN's beta replaces it.

9:00 RECEIPT — bn = nn.BatchNorm1d(200); x = torch.randn(32, 200). torch.testing.assert_close(my_bn(x, training=True), bn.train()(x)); then assert_close(my_running_var, bn.running_var); then bn.eval() and compare again on a new batch. ln = nn.LayerNorm(200); torch.testing.assert_close(my_ln(x), ln(x)). Both at default rtol/atol for float32.

10:30 MEASURE — The batch-dependence demo: run the same example inside two different batches through BN in train mode, outputs differ; through LN, identical to 0. Then the MLP LM with BN: val loss and the hpreact histogram staying unit-Gaussian.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Normalization axis decides everything: BN couples examples, LN doesn't, so LN works for batch size 1, variable lengths and autoregressive decoding. Interview line: BN behaves differently in train and eval, LN does not, and that asymmetry is a classic production bug.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Residual connections.
key_math: y = gamma (x - mu)/sqrt(var + eps) + beta;  BN: mu,var over batch dim (per feature);  LN: mu,var over feature dim (per example);  running = (1-m) running + m * batch_stat, m=0.1
code_task: norms.py: batchnorm_forward(x (N,C), gamma (C,), beta (C,), running_mean, running_var, training, momentum=0.1, eps=1e-5) -> (N,C); layernorm_forward(x (...,C), gamma, beta, eps=1e-5) -> (...,C). Plug BN into the MLP LM after W1 with b1 removed.
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(my_bn(x, training=True), nn.BatchNorm1d(200).train()(x)); running_var equals bn.running_var after one step (which uses unbiased variance); eval-mode outputs match; torch.testing.assert_close(my_ln(x), nn.LayerNorm(200)(x)).
gotchas: Using unbiased variance for normalization (PyTorch normalizes with the biased var but tracks the unbiased one in running_var); forgetting model.eval() so BN keeps using batch stats at inference; keeping b1 before BN, it is subtracted out and its gradient is exactly zero
interview_q: Why do transformers use LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm? Answer: LayerNorm normalizes each token over its own features, so it is independent of batch size, sequence padding and other examples, and it behaves identically at train and inference; BatchNorm statistics are noisy with small or variable batches and leak information across examples.
explainer: Here are our activations as a grid. Each row is one example. Each column is one feature.
BatchNorm looks down each column. It computes a mean and variance over the batch, then normalizes that feature.
LayerNorm looks across each row. One example, its own mean and variance, normalized on its own.
Same formula for both. Subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation, then a learned scale and shift.
Watch what happens when we move one example into a different batch. BatchNorm changes its output.
LayerNorm gives the exact same output in both batches, because it never looked at the neighbors.
At inference, BatchNorm needs running averages from training. LayerNorm needs nothing. That is why transformers use it.
explainer_visuals: A 6 by 8 grid of colored cells with 'examples' labeling rows and 'features' labeling columns.
A vertical highlight sweeps across columns one at a time, each showing mu and sigma below it.
A horizontal highlight sweeps down rows, each showing mu and sigma to the right.
The equation y = gamma (x - mu)/sqrt(var + eps) + beta, with gamma and beta glowing as learnable.
The same highlighted row placed in two different grids; its BN output colors differ between the two.
The same row's LN output, identical in both grids, with an equals sign between them.
A BN box with a 'running stats' side tank versus an LN box with none; a check mark next to LN and 'transformer'.
short: Same example, two batches, two different BN outputs (MEASURE). Caption: 'BatchNorm makes your output depend on strangers'
yt_title: BatchNorm vs LayerNorm from Scratch: why transformers use LayerNorm
x_post: BatchNorm and LayerNorm are the same formula over different axes. BN couples examples in a batch and needs running stats at eval; LN doesn't. Built both from scratch, allclose to nn.BatchNorm1d and nn.LayerNorm. Code + video: [link]
linkedin: Implemented BatchNorm and LayerNorm from scratch and matched nn.BatchNorm1d (including running stats in train and eval mode) and nn.LayerNorm. The demo that made it click: one example's BN output changes depending on its batchmates, while LN's is identical. That independence is why transformers use LayerNorm.

hook: Delete one plus sign from a 50-layer network and the first layer's gradient drops by orders of magnitude. That plus sign is the residual connection.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Remove one plus sign from a 50-layer network and its first layer stops learning. That plus sign is the residual connection.

0:15 QUESTION — GPT-3 has 96 layers. Llama 3 405B has 126. Without residual connections nobody could train networks this deep, as ResNet showed in 2015. Every transformer block is literally x = x + attention(x) followed by x = x + mlp(x).

1:00 INTUITION — Without a residual, the gradient to layer 1 is a product of 50 Jacobians. Products of many numbers either vanish or explode. With x + f(x), every layer gets an identity path straight back to the loss: a gradient highway with on-ramps. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Plain: x_{l+1} = f_l(x_l), so dL/dx_1 = dL/dx_L * prod_{l} J_l. If the typical singular value of J_l is 0.9, after 50 layers you get 0.9^50 = 0.005. Residual: x_{l+1} = x_l + f_l(x_l), so J = I + J_f and dL/dx_1 = dL/dx_L * prod (I + J_{f,l}). Expanding the product, the identity term always survives, so the gradient never vanishes. Cost: the residual stream variance grows with depth, about L times, which is why GPT-2 scales residual projection init by 1/sqrt(2L).

6:00 CODE — class Block(nn.Module): __init__(d, residual): self.ln = nn.LayerNorm(d); self.fc = nn.Linear(d, d). forward(x): y = torch.tanh(self.fc(self.ln(x))); return x + y if residual else y. class DeepMLP(depth=50, d=128, residual). Task: the char MLP LM with these blocks between embedding and head. After loss.backward(), collect [blk.fc.weight.grad.norm().item() for blk in model.blocks]. Train both variants 5k steps with Adam lr 1e-3.

9:30 RECEIPT — Per-layer grad norms: residual net ratio grad_norm[0]/grad_norm[-1] within about 10x; plain net ratio below 1e-3, the early layers effectively frozen. Loss: residual depth 50 trains to roughly the same val loss as a depth 4 net; plain depth 50 stalls near ln(27) = 3.30 for a long time. Also verify the identity-path claim: with all fc weights zeroed, the residual net's output equals its input exactly, assert torch.equal(block(x), x).
10:45 MEASURE — Log-scale plot of grad norm vs layer index for both nets; loss curves for depth 50 with and without residuals; residual stream norm growing with depth.

11:45 TAKEAWAY — Residuals turn a product of Jacobians into a sum of paths, so depth stops killing gradients. Interview line: in a transformer, each sublayer reads from and writes to the residual stream with a plus, which is also what makes it interpretable.
12:15 NEXT — Next: Backprop by hand for a whole MLP LM.
key_math: plain: dL/dx_1 = dL/dx_L prod_l J_l;  residual: x_{l+1} = x_l + f(x_l), J = I + J_f;  0.9^50 approx 0.005
code_task: residual.py: Block(d, residual: bool) with pre-LayerNorm, Linear(d,d), tanh; DeepMLP(depth=50, d=128) on the char LM, x (B, 3*emb) -> (B, d) -> blocks -> head (B, 27); grad_norms(model) -> list of 50 floats after one backward.
receipt: Plain depth-50: grad_norms[0]/grad_norms[-1] < 1e-3; residual: ratio within ~10x; with fc weights and biases zeroed, torch.equal(block(x), x) for the residual block; residual depth-50 val loss within 0.05 of depth-4.
gotchas: Measuring grad norm before backward or after optimizer.step, so you see zeros or post-update values; adding the residual around the LayerNorm too, x + ln(x), which is not the standard form; comparing nets at different learning rates and attributing the gap to residuals
interview_q: Why can you train a 100-layer transformer but not a 100-layer plain MLP? Answer: residual connections make each layer's Jacobian I + J_f, so the gradient has an identity path to every layer and does not decay as a product of many factors; normalization keeps the forward activations in range.
explainer: Here is a fifty layer network with no shortcuts. Each layer only sees the output of the one before it.
Backprop multiplies the gradient by each layer's Jacobian on the way down. Fifty multiplications in a row.
If each factor is zero point nine, fifty of them leave you with half a percent. The bottom layers barely move.
Now add one plus sign per layer. The output becomes the input plus whatever the layer adds.
The Jacobian becomes identity plus the layer's part. The identity path carries gradient straight down, untouched.
Here are the measured gradient norms per layer, on a log scale. Plain network in red, residual in blue.
Every transformer block is built on this. Attention adds to the stream, the MLP adds to the stream.
explainer_visuals: A tall vertical stack of 50 thin boxes connected by single arrows.
A red gradient bar descends the stack, shrinking a little at each box, labeled times J.
The calculation 0.9^50 = 0.005 appears; the red bar at the bottom is a thin sliver.
Each box gets a bypass arrow curving around it, merging at a plus node.
A bright straight line runs down the bypass side of the stack, the red bar staying full width along it.
A log-scale line chart, x axis layer 1 to 50; the red line dives five orders of magnitude, the blue stays nearly flat.
The stack morphs into transformer blocks, each with attention and MLP side branches writing into one central vertical stream.
short: Grad norm per layer log plot (MEASURE). Caption: 'One plus sign keeps 50 layers alive'
yt_title: Residual Connections Explained: gradient flow in a 50-layer net
x_post: 0.9^50 = 0.005. That's why deep plain nets don't train. Residuals make each Jacobian I + J_f, so gradient has a highway. Measured it: plain 50-layer net, layer-1 grad 1000x smaller than layer-50; residual, nearly flat. Code + video: [link]
linkedin: Measured gradient flow in a 50-layer MLP with and without residual connections. Without them, the first layer's gradient norm was over 1000x smaller than the last layer's and training stalled; with them, the per-layer norms were nearly flat. This is the reason every transformer block is x + f(x).

hook: I'm going to write every gradient of a language model by hand, with no autograd, and check each one against PyTorch. All of them match.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — No loss.backward(). I'm writing every gradient of a language model by hand, then checking each one against PyTorch.

0:15 QUESTION — Autograd is a leaky abstraction. When a kernel engineer writes a fused cross-entropy or a FlashAttention backward, there is no autograd underneath. Karpathy calls this becoming a backprop ninja, and interviewers ask you to derive these on a whiteboard.

1:00 INTUITION — Run the forward pass broken into tiny named steps, keep every intermediate, then walk backwards. Each step is one local rule: matmul, add with broadcast, tanh, and cross-entropy. The shape of every gradient equals the shape of the thing it is the gradient of. Use that to check yourself. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Forward: emb = C[Xb] (B,3,d); embcat (B,3d); h_pre = embcat W1 + b1 (B,H); h = tanh(h_pre); logits = h W2 + b2 (B,V); loss = CE. Backward: dlogits = (softmax(logits) - onehot(Y)) / B. dW2 = h^T dlogits (H,V). db2 = dlogits.sum(0). dh = dlogits W2^T (B,H). dh_pre = (1 - h^2) * dh. dW1 = embcat^T dh_pre. db1 = dh_pre.sum(0). dembcat = dh_pre W1^T, reshape to (B,3,d). dC: scatter-add each demb[i,j] into row Xb[i,j]. Rule for broadcasts: if a tensor was broadcast in forward, sum over that dimension in backward.

7:00 CODE — Forward with retain_grad() on every intermediate for checking. def cmp(name, dt, t): ex = torch.all(dt == t.grad).item(); app = torch.allclose(dt, t.grad); maxdiff = (dt - t.grad).abs().max().item(); print it. Write dlogits = F.softmax(logits, 1); dlogits[range(B), Yb] -= 1; dlogits /= B. Then each line from MATH. For dC: dC = torch.zeros_like(C); dC.index_add_(0, Xb.view(-1), demb.view(-1, d)).

10:00 RECEIPT — For each of logits, h, h_pre, W2, b2, W1, b1, embcat, emb, C: cmp() prints approximate: True with maxdiff under about 1e-8 to 1e-9 in float32 and exact: True for several. Final assert: all(torch.allclose(mine[k], p.grad, atol=1e-6) for k, p in params.items()). Bonus: train 10k steps with only manual gradients, no backward call, wrapped in torch.no_grad(); val loss matches the autograd run.
11:30 MEASURE — The cmp table on screen, every row green. Then the loss curve from manual-gradient training overlaid on the autograd one.

12:15 TAKEAWAY — Backprop is local rules plus bookkeeping, and the shape of each gradient tells you what the rule must be. Interview line: the cross-entropy gradient w.r.t. logits is (softmax - onehot) / B, and fusing it is why fused CE kernels save so much memory.
12:45 NEXT — Next: Why tokenization exists.
key_math: dlogits = (softmax(z) - Y)/B;  dW = X^T dY, dX = dY W^T, db = sum_0 dY;  dtanh: dx = (1 - y^2) dy;  embedding: dC[ix] += demb
code_task: backprop_ninja.py: manual_backward(cache) -> dict of grads for C (V,d), W1 (3d,H), b1 (H,), W2 (H,V), b2 (V,) and intermediates; cmp(name, dt, t) helper; manual-gradient training loop under torch.no_grad(). B=32, d=10, H=64, V=27.
receipt: For every param and intermediate: torch.allclose(manual_grad, t.grad) is True with maxdiff < 1e-6 (float32), checked by cmp(); a 10k-step training run using only manual gradients reaches the same val loss as autograd within 0.01.
gotchas: Forgetting to divide dlogits by B because F.cross_entropy averages; summing over the wrong axis for a broadcast bias (db must have the bias's shape); using dC[Xb] += demb, which does not accumulate repeated indices, instead of index_add_
interview_q: Derive the gradient of mean cross-entropy loss with respect to the logits for a batch. Answer: dL/dz = (softmax(z) - onehot(y)) / B, because d/dz_k of -log softmax(z)_y is p_k - 1[k=y] and the mean contributes 1/B.
explainer: Here is our language model's forward pass, written out as a chain of small steps with every intermediate kept.
We start at the loss and go backwards. The first gradient is softmax minus one hot, over the batch size.
A matrix multiply has two gradients. Each is the incoming gradient times the transpose of the other input.
The bias was broadcast across the batch going forward, so going backward we sum over the batch.
Tanh is easy. Its derivative is one minus the output squared, multiplied element by element.
The embedding table gets gradients only in the rows we looked up. Repeated letters add up.
Every one of our hand written gradients matches PyTorch. Green across the board, differences around ten to the minus nine.
